en: The Sūtra on the Emptiness of the Five Aggregates Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by imperial decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park of the Ṛṣipatana.
While staying in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, the World-Honored One addressed the five bhikṣus, saying:
"You should know this: form is not the self. If form were the self, form would not be subject to sickness or suffering."
"I desire such form; I do not desire such form.
Since it is not as one wishes, according to one's desires, one should know that form is not the self;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Furthermore, bhikṣus!
What do you think?
Is form permanent?
"Is this impermanent? He replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
"Form is impermanent.
The Buddha said:
"Since form is impermanent, it is suffering—whether it be the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, or the suffering of conditioned formations."
However, do my many-hearing śrāvaka disciples cling to the existence of a self?
Do they hold that form is the self, that the self possesses form, that form belongs to the self, or that the self dwells within form?
"No, World-Honored One! You should know that feeling,
perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise both permanent and impermanent."
Whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; superior or inferior; far or near—all of it is entirely without self.

"You all should know that you must skillfully observe with right wisdom; in this way, all feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—past, future, and present—all should be observed with right wisdom as previously described."

If my noble disciples, the śrāvakas, contemplate these five aggregates of clinging and know that there is no self nor anything belonging to a self; having contemplated thus, they know that in the world there is neither a grasper nor that which is grasped, nor is there any transformation; rather, through their own awakening, they realize nirvāṇa, [knowing]: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
When this Dharma was taught, the minds of the five bhikṣus and others were liberated from all afflictions; they received it with faith and practiced accordingly.
*The Sūtra on the Emptiness of the Five Aggregates Spoken by the Buddha*.
